turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late, I was stuck on the M50, sat there near twenty minutes. The traffic was desperate.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah you're grand altogether, don't be worrying. Filthy day for driving.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): It is yeah. Rain hasn't let up since Tuesday and I left the good coat in the house.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Were you out in that on Sunday for the match?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I was, up in the stand, soaked through. Dublin were poor in the second half, I thought they'd never score.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah they left it very late. My brother was roaring at the telly the whole time. Sure look, you're here now. What brought you in?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, well, um, it's the hands. They go numb at night.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which fingers, and is it the two hands?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly the right. The thumb, the index and the middle one. I do be waking with it and I have to shake the hand to get the feeling back.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, I haven't a clue of the date. A few months anyway. Maybe since the spring, I'm not sure.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how are they in the daytime?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Daytime they're mostly grand, but I've started dropping cups. Dropped a mug of tea yesterday, all over the kitchen floor.
[SEG0014] person_3 (NURSE): Sorry for barging in. I'll just do the blood pressure. My own sister had the numb fingers last year, shaking her hands out at breakfast, her husband was driven demented.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): God, was she alright? Am I going to lose the use of the hand? I keep panicking.
[SEG0016] person_3 (NURSE): She was grand after. Yours is 138 over 86, and the pulse is 74. I'll leave ye to it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Any pain in the neck?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No pain in the neck.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in the legs, or pins and needles in the feet?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No, the legs are fine, and there's nothing in the feet. Uh, is this a stroke? I was reading things at half two and I frightened the life out of myself.

[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): I don't think this is a stroke, let me think it through. Numb thumb, index and middle finger at night, you shake it awake, you're dropping cups. Could be the nerve at the wrist, could be a nerve from the neck, could be a bit of arthritis in the hand. I'm not going to call it the neck just yet.

[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): If I'm right, the median nerve is getting pinched in the little tunnel at the wrist. That nerve looks after those three fingers, so they go dead, and the little finger is usually spared because a different nerve minds it.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): So not the brain? Will I need an operation? How serious is it really?
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): My working impression is carpal tunnel. A pinched nerve from the neck is still possible, I wouldn't rule that out. There's no operation talk today.

[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look. Sensation is a bit dull over the right thumb and index. Tinel's, tapping at the wrist, sends a tingle into those fingers. The little finger feels normal and the grip is decent.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Is dull bad? I work in accounts, typing all day. Do I have to give up the job?

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, don't be giving up the job. A wrist splint at night is the first thing, for six weeks, keeps the wrist straight so the nerve isn't bent up. You can get one in the chemist, no bother.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Every single night? And if I need the nerve test, does it hurt? The neighbour said they stick needles in you and I'm fairly worked up about that.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not booking a nerve conduction study today. If the numbness hasn't settled in six weeks, then we'd arrange the nerve test. It's mostly little electrical taps on the skin, not a big needle job, people are grand with it.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): And what if it is the neck after all? Should I be on tablets? I take paracetemol now and again, two tablets, when the hand gets sore. Not every day.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's why I won't lock it down further today, we'll see how the splint goes. Paracetamol as needed is fine, nothing stronger for now. Come back and see me in six weeks.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): And if the hand goes properly weak, or you can't hold a cup at all, come back sooner, don't wait.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Six weeks. I'll try not to be googling it at half two. Thanks.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Mind yourself on that motorway going home.

spec.situation: Middle-aged office or factory worker with night-time numbness in thumb, index and middle fingers, shakes hands to wake them; dropping cups; splint advice, nerve test conditional.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

omissions.text: Possible differential of arthritis in the hand was mentioned by the doctor ('could be a bit of arthritis in the hand').
Doctor advised a wrist splint specifically to keep the wrist straight so the nerve isn't bent up, and said it can be bought at the chemist.
Doctor stated that little finger is usually spared in carpal tunnel because it is supplied by a different nerve.
Doctor reassured that this did not sound like a stroke ('I don't think this is a stroke').
Doctor advised no operation talk today / no operation planned at this stage.
Doctor explained that the nerve conduction study was not being booked today and described it as mostly little electrical taps on the skin, not a big needle job.
